project.name: agenticengineering-nl
project.description: Marketing and intake site for the Agentic Engineering training programme — bilingual (NL/EN), dark terminal-native aesthetic, built on Next.js 15 App Router and deployed on Vercel. Includes a news/articles surface and a bilingual blog subsystem.

nodes.name: page.tsx
nodes.summary: Dynamic blog post detail page (RSC) for the localized articles route; statically generates one path per locale/slug and renders a single blog post fetched by slug, calling notFound() when missing.

nodes.name: generateStaticParams
nodes.summary: Builds the static param set by mapping every blog slug across every configured locale for prerendering the blog detail route.

nodes.name: BlogPostPage
nodes.summary: Async server component that resolves the locale, loads the blog by slug via getBlogBySlug, and renders the post or triggers a 404.

nodes.name: page.tsx
nodes.summary: Articles index page (RSC) that merges external news articles and internal blog posts into a single date-sorted timeline and renders each via TimelineEntryRow.

nodes.name: ArticlesPage
nodes.summary: Async server component that fetches articles and blogs, tags and merges them into a unified timeline sorted by date, then maps over the entries to render the localized articles listing.

nodes.name: ArticleCard.tsx
nodes.summary: Presentational card for an external news Article, truncating the summary and linking out to the original source with localized labels.

nodes.name: ArticleCard
nodes.summary: Renders a single external article card with a truncated 400-char summary and a localized read-more link to the source URL.

nodes.name: BlogCard.tsx
nodes.summary: Presentational card for an internal Blog post, linking to the localized blog detail route with a localized read-more label.

nodes.name: BlogCard
nodes.summary: Renders a single blog post card with title, summary and a localized Link into the article detail page.

nodes.name: TimelineEntry.tsx
nodes.summary: Unified timeline row component that discriminates between a blog entry and an external article entry, rendering the appropriate layout with localized labels.

nodes.name: TimelineEntryRow
nodes.summary: Renders one timeline entry, branching on entry.kind ('blog' vs 'article') to show either an internal blog link or an outbound source link, using separate blog and article translation namespaces.

nodes.name: articles.ts
nodes.summary: Server-side loader that reads the news markdown directory, validates each file's frontmatter with a Zod schema, and returns a date-sorted list of external news Article objects.

nodes.name: getArticles
nodes.summary: Reads markdown files from the news directory, parses and Zod-validates frontmatter, derives a slug from the filename, and returns the validated articles sorted newest-first.

nodes.name: blogs.ts
nodes.summary: Server-side loader for the bilingual blog subsystem: reads per-locale markdown files, validates frontmatter, pairs NL/EN variants by slug, enforces shared-field parity, and exposes getBlogs and getBlogBySlug.

nodes.name: sharedFieldEqual
nodes.summary: Compares a shared frontmatter field (scalar or array) between two locale variants for strict equality, used to enforce NL/EN parity.

nodes.name: parseBlogFile
nodes.summary: Reads a single blog markdown file, parses its frontmatter, and validates it against the Zod frontmatter schema, throwing with file context on failure.

nodes.name: getBlogs
nodes.summary: Scans the blogs directory for locale-suffixed markdown files, groups them by slug, validates both NL and EN exist with matching shared fields, and returns the assembled bilingual blog list sorted by date.

nodes.name: getBlogBySlug
nodes.summary: Convenience lookup that returns the single blog whose slug matches, delegating to getBlogs.

nodes.name: parseFrontmatter.ts
nodes.summary: Small utility that extracts and parses YAML frontmatter from a raw markdown string using js-yaml, returning the parsed object plus the body.

nodes.name: parseFrontmatter
nodes.summary: Matches the leading YAML frontmatter block of a markdown string, parses it with js-yaml, and returns the data object alongside the remaining body.

tour.title: Project Overview & Brand
tour.description: Start with the README to learn what this is: the bilingual (NL/EN) marketing and intake site for the Agentic Engineering training programme, built on Next.js 15 App Router and deployed on Vercel. PRODUCT.md captures who the site is for and its tone of voice, while DESIGN.md defines the dark, terminal-native visual system. Together these three documents are the roadmap for everything the tour covers next.

tour.title: Locale Routing Entry Point
tour.description: Every request enters through middleware.ts, the true entry point of the app. It runs next-intl's locale middleware so a bare '/' redirects to the default Dutch locale '/nl' and all routes become locale-scoped (/nl/*, /en/*). The path matcher config decides which requests the middleware touches versus passing straight through to static assets.
tour.languageLesson: Next.js middleware runs on every matched request before rendering. The exported `config.matcher` regex is what keeps it off static assets and API internals — a common performance footgun if it is too broad.

tour.title: The i18n Foundation
tour.description: Building on the middleware from Step 2, this is the bilingual machinery the whole site rests on. routing.ts is the single source of truth for supported locales and the NL default; request.ts resolves the active locale per request and loads the matching message bundle. The nl.json and en.json catalogs hold every piece of UI copy, kept at strict key parity (CI enforces it) so neither language can drift.

tour.title: Layout & Chrome
tour.description: The locale layout is the shell every page renders inside. It validates the incoming locale, sets the request locale for next-intl, generates per-locale SEO metadata, and wraps each page in the persistent Nav and Footer. The LangSwitcher lets visitors flip between NL and EN while preserving their current path.

tour.title: The Home Page
tour.description: The home page is a React Server Component that composes the marketing surface: the Hero, a ProofStrip of social proof, the training listings, an instructor grid, and JSON-LD structured data for SEO. It is the highest-fan-out page in the app, pulling together components and data introduced in the next steps.
tour.languageLesson: React Server Components (RSC) render on the server with zero client JS by default. Interactive pieces (like the contact form later) opt into the client with a `'use client'` directive — the rest stays server-only for speed and SEO.

tour.title: Training Catalogue
tour.description: The training programme content lives as typed static data in data/trainings.ts (modules, pricing) and data/instructors.ts. TrainingCard renders the compact listing on the home page, while TrainingDetail expands the full curriculum, outcomes, audience and pricing. This data module has one of the highest fan-in counts in the codebase — cards, detail views and tests all consume it.

tour.title: Articles & Blog Subsystem
tour.description: The newest surface merges two content sources into one timeline. lib/articles.ts loads external news links from markdown, while lib/blogs.ts loads the internal bilingual blog, pairing NL/EN markdown variants by slug and enforcing shared-field parity; both lean on parseFrontmatter.ts for YAML parsing. The /articles index page date-sorts everything and renders each row through TimelineEntry, which discriminates between an internal BlogCard and an outbound ArticleCard.
tour.languageLesson: TimelineEntry is a discriminated union in action: a single `type` field on the entry lets TypeScript narrow each row to either a Blog or an Article shape, so the component renders the right layout with full type safety.

tour.title: Article Image Pipeline
tour.description: External news links need preview images, fetched at build time rather than at runtime. scripts/fetch-article-images.ts drives a headless Chromium (Playwright) to scrape OpenGraph images, but only from hosts in the trusted-domains.json allowlist — a deliberate SSRF guardrail — falling back to a local icon when an image is unavailable.

tour.title: The Contact Pipeline
tour.description: The intake form is the site's one truly interactive flow and its most security-sensitive path. ContactForm is a client component using react-hook-form with a Zod resolver that shares lib/validation.ts with the server. The POST handler in route.ts layers defenses in order — same-origin check, per-IP rate limiting, honeypot, then Zod validation — before lib/email.ts dispatches via Resend; lib/sanitize.ts strips CRLF to block header injection and lib/rate-limit.ts holds the in-memory token buckets.
tour.languageLesson: Sharing one Zod schema between client and server gives a single source of truth for validation: the browser gets instant feedback and the API independently re-validates, so a tampered request can never bypass the rules.

tour.title: Design Tokens & Build Config
tour.description: The dark terminal aesthetic from DESIGN.md is implemented in globals.css using Tailwind v4's @theme block as the single source of design tokens (OKLCH colors, JetBrains Mono / Inter fonts) plus focus-visible and reduced-motion handling. next.config.ts wires in the next-intl plugin and the production-only security headers (HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options) documented in the README.
tour.languageLesson: Tailwind v4 moves design tokens into a CSS-native `@theme` block instead of a JS config file — utilities are generated directly from those custom properties, so the stylesheet itself becomes the design system's source of truth.

tour.title: CI Quality Gate
tour.description: The capstone is how every change is kept honest. The CI workflow runs on each push and PR with parallel jobs — lint, typecheck, the verify:i18n parity gate, coverage tests, build, plus dependency audits. scripts/verify-i18n.ts is the script behind that gate, comparing nl.json and en.json key-for-key so a missing translation fails CI rather than shipping a blank string. This closes the loop from the i18n foundation in Step 3.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions split work into parallel `jobs`, each a sequence of `steps`. Running lint, typecheck and tests as independent jobs means they execute concurrently and report failures independently, shortening feedback time on a PR.
